entries.meaning: To find someone or something pleasant or enjoyable. ---
examples: I like your new haircut.
She liked the movie much more than the book.
He has always liked working outdoors.

entries.meaning: To feel deep affection or very strong liking for someone or something. ---
examples: They love their grandchildren more than anything.
I loved that little restaurant downtown.
She has loved the ocean since she was a child.

entries.meaning: To get pleasure from something. ---
examples: We enjoy long walks after dinner.
I enjoyed every minute of the concert.
The kids are enjoying the warm weather.
entries.contrast: Followed by -ing, never by to: I enjoy reading, not I enjoy to read.

entries.meaning: To love someone or something very much. ---
examples: The kids adore their new puppy.
She adored her grandfather.
He has adored jazz since he was a teenager.

entries.meaning: To respect and think highly of someone, or to look at something with pleasure. ---
examples: I admire her patience with the students.
We admired the view from the bridge for a while.
He has always admired his older sister.

entries.meaning: To be grateful for something, or to recognize its true value. ---
examples: I really appreciate your help with the move.
She appreciated the honest feedback.
He has never appreciated how much work goes into it.

entries.meaning: To care for something deeply and keep it precious. ---
examples: They cherish the time they get together.
She cherished every letter he sent.
It is a memory he has cherished for forty years.

entries.meaning: To admire someone's qualities, or to accept their rights and wishes. ---
examples: Students respect her because she is fair.
He respected their decision even though he disagreed.
She has been respected by her colleagues for years.

entries.meaning: To consider something important and worth having. ---
examples: We value your feedback.
She valued his honesty above everything else.
He has always valued loyalty in a friend.

entries.meaning: To keep something as very precious because of what it means to you. ---
examples: I treasure the letters my mother wrote.
She treasured that old photograph.
He has treasured the watch since his father gave it to him.

entries.meaning: To dislike someone or something very strongly. ---
examples: I hate getting up before six.
She hated the noise from the street.
He has hated flying since he was a kid.

entries.meaning: To find someone or something unpleasant. ---
examples: I dislike crowded places.
She disliked him from the first meeting.
They have always disliked the new rules.
entries.contrast: Always needs an object: I dislike it, not I dislike.

entries.meaning: To look down on someone or something with strong contempt. ---
examples: He despises dishonesty of any kind.
She despised the way they treated the staff.
He has despised that company for years.

entries.meaning: To hate something intensely. ---
examples: I detest cold coffee.
She detested every minute of the trip.
He has detested public speaking all his life.

entries.meaning: To feel disgust and hatred for someone or something. ---
examples: I loathe the smell of gasoline.
She loathed her old job.
He has loathed early mornings since college.
entries.contrast: The verb loathe /loʊð/ is not the adjective loath /loʊθ/, which means 'unwilling'.

entries.meaning: To feel bitter about something you think is unfair. ---
examples: She resents being told what to wear.
He resented the extra work at first.
They have resented that decision for years.

entries.meaning: To make someone feel strong dislike and revulsion. ---
examples: Cruelty to animals disgusts me.
The state of the kitchen disgusted her.
He was disgusted by what he read online.

entries.meaning: To make someone suddenly afraid. ---
examples: Loud noises scare the dog.
You scared me half to death.
He is scaring the children with that mask.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (you scared me), intransitive (she scares easily)
entries.contrast: The feeling takes of: She's scared of spiders.

entries.meaning: To make someone feel fear. ---
examples: Thunderstorms frighten the baby.
The sudden noise frightened her.
He has never been frightened by the dark.

entries.meaning: To fill someone with extreme fear. ---
examples: Snakes terrify my brother.
The turbulence terrified the passengers.
She was terrified of losing her job.
entries.contrast: The -y becomes -ies and -ied: terrifies, terrified — but terrifying keeps the y.

entries.meaning: To feel anxious fear about something that is coming. ---
examples: I dread Monday mornings.
She dreaded the phone call all week.
He has been dreading this meeting for days.
entries.contrast: Usually followed by -ing: I dread telling him.

entries.meaning: To make someone suddenly worried or frightened. ---
examples: The test results alarm her doctor.
The news alarmed everyone in the office.
We were alarmed by how fast the fire spread.

entries.meaning: To surprise someone so suddenly that they jump. ---
examples: Don't startle him while he's driving.
The cat startled me when it jumped down.
She was startled by a knock at the door.

entries.meaning: To shock someone deeply and unpleasantly. ---
examples: Those photos horrify everyone who sees them.
His answer horrified the audience.
She was horrified to learn the truth.
entries.contrast: The -y changes: horrifies, horrified, but horrifying.

entries.meaning: To feel or cause sudden uncontrollable fear. ---
examples: Try not to panic if the alarm goes off.
She panicked when she couldn't find her passport.
Half the crowd was panicking by then.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the rumor panicked investors), intransitive (don't panic)
entries.contrast: A k is added before the ending: panicked, panicking — never paniced.

entries.meaning: To shake slightly from fear, cold, or strong emotion. ---
examples: His hands tremble when he is nervous.
She trembled as she opened the envelope.
He stood there trembling with rage.

entries.meaning: To shake a little because you are cold or afraid. ---
examples: I shiver every time I step outside.
The children shivered in the wind.
She was shivering by the time we got home.

entries.meaning: To worry continuously about small things. ---
examples: Don't fret about the details.
She fretted all night over the results.
He was fretting about money again.
entries.contrast: Doubles the t: fretted, fretting.

entries.meaning: To lose all hope. ---
examples: Don't despair — there is still time.
She despaired of ever finding a job.
He had almost despaired when the letter came.
entries.contrast: Takes of: despair of ever finishing.

entries.meaning: To think about one thing constantly and be unable to stop. ---
examples: Try not to obsess over one bad review.
The mystery obsessed him for years.
She has been obsessing about the interview all week.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the idea obsessed him), intransitive (stop obsessing)
entries.contrast: The adjective takes with: She's obsessed with that show.

entries.meaning: To make someone feel wonder because something was unexpected. ---
examples: Her answer surprises nobody.
The ending surprised everybody in the theater.
We were surprised by how cold it was.
entries.contrast: Surprised by an event, surprised at someone's behavior.

entries.meaning: To fill someone with great surprise and wonder. ---
examples: Your energy amazes me.
The size of the canyon amazed them.
She has amazed her teachers all year.

entries.meaning: To surprise someone very greatly. ---
examples: His memory astonishes me.
The result astonished the experts.
We were astonished to see snow in April.

entries.meaning: To upset or offend someone with something sudden and unexpected. ---
examples: Nothing shocks her anymore.
The verdict shocked the whole town.
They were shocked by the price of the tickets.

entries.meaning: To surprise someone so much that they cannot react. ---
examples: The news will stun his fans.
Her question stunned the whole room.
He sat there, stunned, for a full minute.
entries.contrast: Doubles the n: stunned, stunning.

entries.meaning: To make someone feel admiration. ---
examples: Her essay impresses every reader.
The chef impressed us with a very simple soup.
We were impressed by how quickly they finished.
entries.contrast: Impressed by or impressed with — never impressed from.

entries.meaning: To make someone feel happy or satisfied. ---
examples: Small things please him.
The gift pleased her enormously.
We were pleased to hear the good news.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the gift pleased her), intransitive (do as you please)

entries.meaning: To give someone great pleasure. ---
examples: Simple magic tricks delight small children.
The concert delighted the whole audience.
She was delighted to get the invitation.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the show delighted us), intransitive (she delights in cooking)
entries.contrast: In the intransitive sense it takes in: He delights in proving people wrong.

entries.meaning: To make someone content by giving them what they want or need. ---
examples: Nothing I do satisfies him.
That answer satisfied the committee.
He has never been satisfied with second place.
entries.contrast: The -y changes: satisfies, satisfied, but satisfying.

entries.meaning: To give someone a sudden feeling of great excitement. ---
examples: Roller coasters thrill him.
The surprise ending thrilled the crowd.
She was thrilled to hear from you.

entries.meaning: To make someone feel eager and full of energy about something. ---
examples: Travel plans always excite the kids.
The announcement excited everyone in the room.
They were excited about the trip for weeks.

entries.meaning: To make someone smile or laugh, or to keep them pleasantly occupied. ---
examples: His stories amuse everyone at the table.
The puppet show amused the children for an hour.
She was not amused by the joke.

entries.meaning: To keep people interested and enjoying themselves. ---
examples: Clowns entertain the crowd between acts.
He entertained us with stories from the road.
The kids were entertaining themselves with a cardboard box.

entries.meaning: To do something enjoyable to mark a happy event. ---
examples: We celebrate Thanksgiving with my in-laws.
They celebrated their anniversary in Chicago.
The whole town was celebrating that night.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (celebrate a birthday), intransitive (let's celebrate)

entries.meaning: To feel and show great joy. ---
examples: The whole town will rejoice at that news.
They rejoiced when the war finally ended.
Fans were rejoicing in the streets.
entries.contrast: Takes at or in: rejoice at the news, rejoice in her success.

entries.meaning: To make someone feel less sad or worried. ---
examples: A warm drink comforts her when she is sad.
He comforted the child until her mother came.
She sat with him, comforting him as best she could.

entries.meaning: To give sympathy to someone who is disappointed or grieving. ---
examples: Nothing I say seems to console her.
He consoled the losing team in the locker room.
She was consoled by how many people came.
entries.contrast: The verb is /kənˈsoʊl/; the noun console (a game console, a control panel) is /ˈkɑːnsoʊl/.

entries.meaning: To calm someone down, or to make a pain feel less sharp. ---
examples: Warm milk soothes him before bed.
She soothed the baby with an old song.
The cream is already soothing the burn.

entries.meaning: To make someone or something quiet and peaceful again. ---
examples: Deep breaths calm her nerves.
He calmed the frightened horse in a minute.
Her voice was calming everyone in the room.
entries.contrast: The l is silent: /kɑːm/, one syllable.

entries.meaning: To become or make less tense and worried. ---
examples: I relax by walking the dog.
We relaxed on the porch all afternoon.
He was finally relaxing after a long week.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the music relaxes me), intransitive (relax for an hour)

entries.meaning: To fill someone with the desire or the ability to do something. ---
examples: Her story inspires young athletes.
The trip inspired him to learn Spanish.
She has inspired a whole generation of writers.

entries.meaning: To give someone a reason to act or to keep trying. ---
examples: Money doesn't motivate everyone.
Her coach motivated her with small weekly goals.
The team has been motivated by last year's loss.

entries.meaning: To make someone slightly angry. ---
examples: Loud chewing annoys me.
His constant texting annoyed the teacher.
She was annoyed that nobody had called.
entries.contrast: Annoyed with a person, annoyed at/by a thing.

entries.meaning: To make someone impatient and annoyed, or to make skin sore. ---
examples: That noise irritates everyone in the office.
His tone irritated her.
The wool sweater is irritating my skin.

entries.meaning: To disturb someone, or to make the effort to do something. ---
examples: Does the noise bother you?
It bothered him that she never replied.
He has been bothering me about it all week.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (don't bother me), intransitive (don't bother)

entries.meaning: To make someone angry. ---
examples: Nothing angers him like unfairness.
The decision angered thousands of people.
Fans were angered by the sudden price hike.

entries.meaning: To make someone extremely angry. ---
examples: Comments like that enrage the whole community.
The verdict enraged the crowd outside.
He was enraged by the accusation.

entries.meaning: To make someone furious. ---
examples: Slow drivers infuriate my father.
Her calm answer infuriated him even more.
It is infuriating to wait this long for a reply.

entries.meaning: To hurt someone's feelings or upset their sense of what is proper. ---
examples: I hope the joke didn't offend anyone.
His remark offended half the room.
She was offended that nobody asked her opinion.

entries.meaning: To deliberately make someone angry, or to cause a strong reaction. ---
examples: Don't provoke the dog.
His speech provoked an angry response.
The film has provoked a lot of debate.

entries.meaning: To complain in an annoying, high, childish voice. ---
examples: The kids whine when they are tired.
He whined about the cold for an hour.
Stop whining and finish your homework.
entries.contrast: In American English it sounds exactly like wine (the drink).

entries.meaning: To make someone sad by failing to be as good as they hoped. ---
examples: I hope the movie doesn't disappoint you.
The second album disappointed his fans.
She was disappointed with her grade.
entries.contrast: One s, two p's: d-i-s-a-pp-o-i-n-t.

entries.meaning: To make someone feel low and without energy. ---
examples: Gray winters depress a lot of people.
The news depressed everyone at the table.
He felt depressed for weeks after the move.

entries.meaning: To make someone feel sad. ---
examples: Stories like that sadden me.
It saddened her to sell the family house.
We were saddened to hear of his death.

entries.meaning: To feel deep sorrow, especially after someone dies. ---
examples: People grieve in very different ways.
He grieved for his mother all that year.
She is still grieving the loss of her dog.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (it grieves me to say it), intransitive (she is still grieving)
entries.contrast: Takes for or over: grieve for a friend.

entries.meaning: To show and feel sorrow for someone who has died. ---
examples: They mourn him every year on that date.
The whole country mourned after the crash.
She is still mourning her brother.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (mourn a friend), intransitive (the country mourned)
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like morn (as in morning).

entries.meaning: To feel sad because someone or something is no longer with you. ---
examples: I miss my family every single day.
She missed her friends terribly that first year.
He has been missing his old neighborhood.

entries.meaning: To produce tears because of sadness, pain, or strong feeling. ---
examples: Some people cry at weddings.
The baby cried most of the night.
She has been crying since she heard.
entries.contrast: The -y becomes -ies and -ied, but stays in crying.

entries.meaning: To cry noisily, taking sharp breaths. ---
examples: He tried not to sob in front of them.
She sobbed into the pillow.
The child was still sobbing an hour later.
entries.contrast: Doubles the b: sobbed, sobbing.

entries.meaning: To feel sorry for someone in a bad situation. ---
examples: Don't pity me — I'm fine.
She pitied him more than she loved him.
He has never pitied anyone in his life.
entries.contrast: The -y changes: pities, pitied, but pitying.

entries.meaning: To understand and share someone's feelings, especially bad ones. ---
examples: I sympathize with anyone who works nights.
She sympathized with the strikers.
He was sympathizing with the wrong side.
entries.contrast: Takes with; American spelling is -ize, British sympathise.

entries.meaning: To imagine and feel what another person is feeling. ---
examples: Good nurses empathize with their patients.
She empathized immediately with the new student.
He has never been good at empathizing.
entries.русский: сопереживать, ставить себя на место другого
entries.contrast: Takes with; American spelling is -ize, British empathise.

entries.meaning: To make someone unable to understand or explain something. ---
examples: Her reaction puzzles me.
The missing key puzzled the detectives.
He was puzzled by the question.

entries.meaning: To confuse someone completely. ---
examples: The symptoms baffle her doctors.
The result baffled everyone.
Scientists have been baffled by the readings.
entries.русский: ставить в тупик, сбивать с толку

entries.meaning: To confuse someone so much that they don't know what to do. ---
examples: Big airports bewilder my grandmother.
The paperwork bewildered him completely.
She looked bewildered by the whole thing.

entries.meaning: To make someone annoyed because they cannot do what they want. ---
examples: Slow internet frustrates everyone.
The delay frustrated the whole team.
He was frustrated that nobody would listen.

entries.meaning: To make someone lose interest and feel tired of something. ---
examples: Long speeches bore me.
The lecture bored half the class to sleep.
She has been bored all week.
entries.contrast: This bore is regular (bored, boring); the identical bore you may also meet is the past of bear.

entries.meaning: To affect someone so strongly that they cannot cope. ---
examples: Big crowds overwhelm him.
The response overwhelmed the little shop.
She was overwhelmed by all the messages.

entries.meaning: To make someone want to know more about something. ---
examples: Politics doesn't interest him at all.
The offer interested her enough to call back.
He has always been interested in old cars.
entries.contrast: The adjective takes in: interested in history.

entries.meaning: To attract and hold someone's interest completely. ---
examples: Bugs fascinate my son.
The documentary fascinated all of us.
She has always been fascinated by space.

entries.meaning: To make someone curious because something is strange or mysterious. ---
examples: The title alone intrigues readers.
His answer intrigued the interviewer.
We were intrigued by the offer.
entries.contrast: The verb stresses the second syllable, /ɪnˈtriːɡ/; the noun is often /ˈɪntriːɡ/.

entries.meaning: To charm someone so much that they cannot look away. ---
examples: Her voice captivates every audience.
The story captivated the whole class.
He was captivated by the city.

entries.meaning: To make someone or something come closer, or to cause liking. ---
examples: Bright colors attract bees.
The festival attracted twenty thousand people.
She was attracted to him from the start.
entries.contrast: The feeling takes to: attracted to someone.

entries.meaning: To please and win someone over with pleasant manners. ---
examples: He charms everyone he meets.
She charmed the whole committee.
They were charmed by the little town.

entries.meaning: To praise someone more than they deserve, often to please them. ---
examples: Don't flatter me — just tell me the truth.
His compliment flattered her.
She was flattered to be asked.

entries.meaning: To make someone feel awkward and self-conscious. ---
examples: Please don't embarrass me in front of my friends.
His question embarrassed her.
She was embarrassed about the mistake for days.
entries.contrast: Two r's and two s's: e-m-b-a-rr-a-ss.

entries.meaning: To make someone feel ashamed and foolish, especially in front of others. ---
examples: Never humiliate a student in public.
The loss humiliated the defending champions.
He felt humiliated by the whole thing.

entries.meaning: To make someone feel ashamed of what they have done. ---
examples: Don't shame people for asking questions.
The article shamed the company into acting.
She was shamed into apologizing.

entries.meaning: To become red in the face from embarrassment. ---
examples: I blush whenever someone compliments me.
She blushed at the question.
He was blushing to the ears.

entries.meaning: To want what someone else has, and feel unhappy about not having it. ---
examples: I envy people who sleep well.
She envied her sister's confidence.
He has always envied their easy life.
entries.contrast: The -y changes: envies, envied, but envying.

entries.meaning: To hold someone close with your arms to show affection. ---
examples: The kids hug their grandpa at the door.
She hugged me for a long time.
They were hugging and crying at the gate.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (hug your mom), intransitive (they hugged)
entries.contrast: Doubles the g: hugged, hugging.

entries.meaning: To touch someone with your lips to show love or greeting. ---
examples: In some countries people kiss on both cheeks.
He kissed her goodbye at the airport.
She was kissing the top of the baby's head.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he kissed her), intransitive (they kissed)

entries.meaning: To accept something unpleasant without complaining or stopping it. ---
examples: I can't tolerate rudeness.
She tolerated the noise for a month before calling the landlord.
He has tolerated far worse than this.

entries.meaning: To suffer something difficult patiently, or to last a long time. ---
examples: Soldiers endure things most of us can't imagine.
She endured six months of treatment.
Their friendship has endured for forty years.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (endure the pain), intransitive (their friendship endured)

entries.meaning: To feel annoyed or bothered by something. ---
examples: I don't mind the cold.
She never minded driving at night.
Would you mind closing the window?
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (I don't mind the cold), intransitive (if you don't mind)
entries.contrast: Do you mind if…? — answering no means 'go ahead'.

entries.meaning: To laugh in a light, nervous, or silly way. ---
examples: The girls giggle through the whole movie.
He giggled at his own joke.
They were giggling in the back row.

entries.meaning: To move your eyebrows together because you are annoyed, worried, or thinking. ---
examples: She frowns when she is concentrating.
He frowned at the bill.
The teacher was frowning at the noise in the back.
entries.contrast: Frown on/upon something means to disapprove of it.

entries.meaning: To make a low sound of pain, annoyance, or disappointment. ---
examples: The students groan every time he says 'pop quiz'.
He groaned when he saw the line at the airport.
The crowd was groaning at every mistake.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like grown (the participle of grow).

entries.meaning: To stay silent and unhappy because you are annoyed about something. ---
examples: He'll sulk for an hour and then forget it.
She sulked all the way home.
He was sulking in his room again.

entries.meaning: To shake suddenly from fear, cold, or disgust. ---
examples: I shudder to think what could have happened.
She shuddered at the sight of the blood.
He was still shuddering from the cold water.

entries.meaning: To keep coming back into someone's mind in a troubling way. ---
examples: Those images still haunt me.
The accident haunted him for years.
She has been haunted by that decision ever since.

entries.meaning: To make someone very upset or anxious. ---
examples: Loud arguments distress the children.
The news distressed her deeply.
He was clearly distressed by the question.

entries.meaning: To cause someone great mental or physical suffering, often repeatedly. ---
examples: Guilt can torment a person for years.
The other boys tormented him at school.
She has been tormented by doubt ever since.
entries.contrast: The verb is /tɔːrˈmɛnt/ (tor-MENT); the noun a torment is /ˈtɔːrmɛnt/ (TOR-ment).

entries.meaning: To interrupt someone, or to make them feel uneasy. ---
examples: Please don't disturb her while she is resting.
The dream disturbed him all day.
We were disturbed by what we saw on the tape.

entries.meaning: To make someone feel shocked disappointment. ---
examples: The numbers dismay even the optimists.
The decision dismayed long-time fans.
She was dismayed to find the store closed.

entries.meaning: To frighten someone, especially into doing what you want.
examples: Big crowds intimidate him.
The lawyer intimidated the witness.
She was intimidated by the interview panel.
